title: How to Price Ocean Freight: A Forwarder’s Method
summary: How to price ocean freight as a forwarder: choose a cost basis, set markup vs margin, manage rate risk between quote and booking. Worked example inside.
body_markdown:
## **How Freight Forwarders Price Ocean Freight: Margins, Markups and Forward Selling**


Here’s how to price ocean freight as a forwarder: take a cost basis (a spot, contract or index-referenced buy rate), add surcharges and local charges, apply a margin rule and set how long the quote holds. The risk sits in the gap between quote and booking.


That gap is what this article calls forward selling: quoting a customer a fixed price for future sailings before you’ve bought the capacity or locked your buy rate.


Below: a five-step quote method, a worked markup vs margin example, and ways to protect margin with 2027 contract talks underway.


## **Start From the Cost Basis: Spot, Contract or Index-Referenced**


The cost basis you pick decides how much of the market’s next move lands on you rather than on your customer.


**Cost basis** **What you know when you quote** **Your exposure** **Typical use**


Spot (carrier or co-loader) Today’s rate for near-term sailings, short validity The rate can move before the customer books One-off shipments, short-validity quotes


Contract (service contract, named account rate, allocation) Base rate for the contract period; surcharges float Allocation cuts, rolled cargo, surcharge resets Regular customers on your core lanes


Consolidator (LCL) Co-loader tariff per weight or measure (W/M), plus local charges Tariff changes, minimums, re-measured cargo LCL customers you don’t consolidate yourself


Index-referenced A formula: index value plus or minus a spread Moves with the index; the spread is fixed Longer agreements that share market moves


A contract rate only protects you if the carrier loads your boxes, and surcharges such as the bunker adjustment factor (BAF) reset on their own schedule even when the base rate holds.


### **Index-Referenced Pricing**


The[Freightos Baltic Index (FBX)](https://www.freightos.com/enterprise/terminal/freightos-baltic-index-global-container-pricing-index/) is a daily index of 40-foot container (FEU) spot prices, published in cooperation with the Baltic Exchange and calculated from real, transacted rates from forwarders and carriers. It covers 12 major ocean lanes plus a Global Container Index, and it’s the only IOSCO-compliant container freight index, used for index-linked contracts and derivatives.


For a forwarder, that’s two uses. A benchmark: check whether your buy and sell rates sit above or below the market. And a contract mechanism: with[index-linked contracts](https://www.freightos.com/logistics-technology-insights/logistics-technology/index-linking-freight-contracts-guide/) , the customer rate resets with the index on an agreed schedule, so a market move is shared instead of absorbed by you.


## **How to Price Ocean Freight: From Buy Rate to Sell Rate**


Pricing desks can work in five steps:


1. **Confirm the all-in buy rate and its validity.** Get the base freight and every carrier surcharge in writing, with the sailing or date range it covers.
2. **Add surcharges and local charges, marked pass-through or fixed.** BAF, peak season surcharges (PSS), general rate increases (GRIs), emergency fuel or war risk surcharges, terminal handling charges (THC) and documentation fees each go on a separate line.
3. **Add your own costs.** Handling, documentation, customs filing, insurance and any trucking you buy in, at what they actually cost you.
4. **Apply your margin rule.** Use the lane and customer policy you’ve set, not a number picked for each quote.
5. **Set validity and conditions.** State the sailing window, how long the price holds and which charges can change.


Step 2 is a common place for margin to leak. If a carrier has announced a GRI that takes effect in two weeks and your quote is valid for 30 days, price it in or exclude it in writing.


For US-licensed NVOCCs quoting under an NVOCC negotiated rate arrangement (NRA), it’s also a compliance point. Under the[Federal Maritime Commission’s NRA rule (46 CFR 532.5)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-46/chapter-IV/subchapter-B/part-532/section-532.5) , an NRA that isn’t all-in must say whether additional surcharges, accessorial charges or ocean carrier GRIs will apply. For a pass-through charge with no specific amount in the NRA or the rules tariff, the NVOCC may invoice only the charge it actually incurs, with no markup.


**What to put on the quote so it holds:** the sailing or cargo-ready window, the validity date, equipment type, whether the rate is all-in, the charges that can change and how you’ll pass them on, included free time, and the rate basis.


### **FCL vs LCL Pricing Logic**


FCL (full container load) is priced per container, so your margin is a dollar figure per box.


LCL (less than container load) is priced per W/M – per cubic meter (CBM) or per 1,000 kg, whichever is greater – usually on a co-loader’s rate plus its local charges and minimums. That makes LCL margin sensitive to declared dimensions, so state that the invoice follows the measured W/M.

## **Ocean Freight Markup vs Margin**


**Markup** is profit as a percentage of your cost. **Margin** is profit as a percentage of your sell rate.


The same percentage gives two different prices. A 20% margin equals a 25% markup, while a 20% markup is only a 16.7% margin. If sales quotes on markup and finance reports on margin, the gap shows up at month end.


- Markup = (sell − cost) ÷ cost
- Margin = (sell − cost) ÷ sell
- Sell rate for a target margin = cost ÷ (1 − margin)


**Illustrative example, hypothetical numbers, not a rate or a benchmark** (one FCL shipment):


**Line** **Priced at 20% markup** **Priced at 20% margin**


All-in buy rate (base freight + carrier surcharges) $2,000 $2,000


Your own costs (documentation, handling) $100 $100


Total cost $2,100 $2,100


Sell rate $2,520 $2,625


Gross profit $420 $525


Margin on sell rate 16.7% 20.0%


Markup on cost 20.0% 25.0%


### **What a Rate Move Does to That Margin**


Now take the 20% margin quote – $2,625, valid for 30 days – before you’ve bought the space. Same hypothetical numbers:


**Buy rate when you book** **Total cost** **Gross profit** **Margin**


Unchanged: $2,000 $2,100 $525 20.0%


Up 10%: $2,200 $2,300 $325 12.4%


Up 20%: $2,400 $2,500 $125 4.8%


Up 30%: $2,600 $2,700 −$75 −2.9%


A 20% rise in the buy rate wipes out more than three-quarters of the gross profit. A 30% rise turns the shipment into a loss. With benchmark rates nearly tripling on one major lane in under six months (see the market snapshot below), that’s not an edge case.


### **Set Margin Policy by Customer and Lane**


Freight forwarder pricing problems are often consistency problems, not arithmetic. Make margin a written policy.


- **Set floors by lane type.** Busy, price-transparent core lanes get lower floors. Thin lanes, special equipment and LCL to secondary ports get higher ones.
- **Adjust by customer, within a band.** Volume commitments and repeat bookings justify a lower margin. A one-off spot request doesn’t.
- **Price the risk.** If the quote runs longer than the buy rate’s validity, add a buffer or shorten the validity.
- **Track dollars per container, not just percentages.** The same dollar profit is a higher percentage when rates fall, and a lower one when they rise.


Without a written rule, you get five sales agents with five slightly different markups. The lanes you quote most are where that drift costs the most.


## **Forward Selling: Pricing Ahead of Your Buy Rate**


Forward selling, as used here, means quoting a customer a fixed price for future sailings before you’ve bought the capacity or locked the buy rate. It isn’t a standard industry term.


Any quote that outlives its buy rate is a bet on the market. If rates fall, you keep the difference. If they rise, you pay it.


The exposure comes from four places:


- **Spot moves** within a quote’s validity, which can reach double digits in peak season.
- **GRIs and PSS** announced after you quote but effective before the sailing.
- **Surcharge resets.**[In June 2026, Freightos Research](https://www.freightos.com/freight-resources/ocean-rates-level-but-mid-month-increases-possible-soon-june-16-2026-update/) noted that large shippers on annual contracts would still pay higher Q3 BAFs even as fuel costs eased, while lower emergency fuel surcharges would help spot shipments .
- **Allocation cuts.** In late[September 2026](https://www.freightos.com/freight-resources/china-us-truce-to-reduce-some-tariffs-and-likely-postpone-port-fees-september-30-2026-update/) , Far East congestion was likely one reason some carriers reduced allocations for some contracted forwarders, according to the Freightos weekly update . A contract rate you can’t load is spot exposure in disguise.


Three ways to manage it:


- **Keep sell validity inside buy validity.** Don’t let a customer quote outlast the buy rate without a buffer or a requote clause.
- **Write pass-through clauses.** Name the charges that pass through at cost (BAF, PSS, GRIs, war risk) and the notice you’ll give. For US NVOCCs, the same FMC rule says NRA amendments apply only to shipments not yet received, so the clause has to be there before the cargo is .
- **[Buy cover](https://www.freightos.com/freight-resources/red-sea-container-traffic-set-for-full-return-in-q1-october-20-2026-update/) .** Back longer fixed quotes with contract rates or allocation on that lane, or move the customer to an index-linked rate.


No cover, a fixed price two months out and carrier increases already announced? Offer a shorter validity or an index-linked rate. A lost quote costs less than a booked loss.


[In October 2026,](https://www.freightos.com/freight-resources/red-sea-container-traffic-set-for-full-return-in-q1-october-20-2026-update/) carriers pushed GRIs on Asia-Europe lanes as 2027 long-term contract negotiations got underway .[On October 9, 2026](https://www.freightos.com/freight-resources/attacks-disrupt-saudi-air-cargo-china-europe-air-rates-slump-october-13-2026-update/) , Asia-N. Europe (FBX11) was $3,260/FEU, 87% above a year earlier, and Asia-Mediterranean (FBX13) $3,804/FEU, up 79%, according to the Freightos Baltic Index. In mid-October, some shippers were hesitant to lock in annual rates at those levels, expecting rates to ease as fleet growth and a Red Sea return add capacity in 2027 . A fixed 2027 price agreed now could land on either side of that bet.


## **Market Snapshot: Ocean Freight Pricing Trends – November 2026**


**Ocean rates – Freightos Baltic Index (index date November 6, 2026)**


- [Asia-US West Coast](https://www.freightos.com/enterprise/terminal/fbx-01-china-to-north-america-west-coast/) prices (FBX01 Weekly) ticked down 1% to $8,245/FEU.
- Asia-US East Coast prices (FBX03 Weekly) were down 2% at $9,708/FEU.
- Asia-N. Europe prices (FBX11 Weekly) fell 5% to $3,422/FEU.
- Asia-Mediterranean prices (FBX13 Weekly) ticked down 1% to $4,324/FEU.
- The Global Container Index (FBX) slipped 2% to $3,452/FEU.


[In the 26 weeks to November 6](https://www.freightos.com/freight-resources/la-lb-strike-deadline-extended-dem-win-increasing-trade-uncertainty-november-10-2026-update/) , Asia-US West Coast prices ran from $2,814/FEU in mid-May to a high of $8,411/FEU in late September, and Asia-Mediterranean prices swung between $3,555/FEU and $7,160/FEU. Transpacific rates eased slightly as significant GRIs failed to materialize but are still at about peak levels, while carriers appear to have abandoned November 1 GRI hopes on Asia-Europe lanes, according to the Freightos weekly update .


For forwarders quoting customers, this means a buy-rate move within one quote’s validity can exceed the whole margin, so validity and pass-through terms deserve as much attention as the sell rate. These index values are market benchmarks, not what Freightos or any forwarder charges.

## **Keep Ocean Quotes Consistent and Fast**


Speed wins quotes; consistency keeps the margin. Both come from setup, not effort.


- **One rate source.** Contract, spot and consolidator rates in one place with their validity dates, not spread across inboxes and PDFs.
- **Update your busiest lanes most often.** The lanes you quote daily are where a stale rate costs most.
- **Apply margin rules in the system.** Lane and customer floors apply automatically, and overrides are logged.
- **Show validity and conditions on every quote.** Same terms from every desk.


[Rate & Quote Ocean](https://www.freightos.com/forwarders/rate-quote/ocean) , part of Freightos for Forwarders, is one way to set this up: it brings live spot and contract rates from ocean liners and LCL consolidators into one view via API, with margin rules applied as you quote. The method works with a disciplined spreadsheet too.


## **The Bottom Line**


Pick the cost basis, build the quote line by line from the all-in buy rate, and apply margin as a written policy. Keep sell validity inside buy validity and name the charges that pass through. When a customer wants a fixed price beyond your cover, price the risk, shorten the term or link it to an index. To run this from one rate source, request a Rate & Quote Ocean demo.


## Frequently Asked Questions


How do freight forwarders make money on ocean freight?


Mainly on the spread between the buy rate from the carrier or co-loader and the sell rate to the customer, plus fees for documentation, customs filing, handling and trucking. Profit is set either as a markup on cost or as a margin on the sell rate. A 25% markup and a 20% margin give the same price.


What is a normal margin on ocean freight?


No single published benchmark holds across lanes, customers and market cycles, so treat quoted industry ranges with caution. Set your own floors instead: lower on competitive core lanes and committed customers, higher on thin lanes, LCL and one-off spot requests. Track gross profit per container alongside the percentage.


How long should an ocean freight quote be valid?


No longer than the buy rate behind it. If the carrier rate is valid for two weeks, a 30-day customer quote carries two weeks of open market risk. Match validity to the buy rate, add a buffer if you must go longer, and name the charges that can change before the sailing.


Should I quote on spot or contract rates?


Quote on the basis you’ll actually ship on. Contract rates suit regular customers on lanes where you have allocation the carrier will honor. Spot suits one-off shipments and lanes without cover. If a customer wants a long fixed price and you have no contract cover, offer an index-linked rate instead.


What happens if the buy rate changes after I quote?


That depends on your quote terms. Without a pass-through or requote clause, the increase comes out of your margin, and a large enough move turns the shipment into a loss. With a clear validity date and named pass-through charges, you can requote or pass the cost on and keep the customer informed.
